segments.text: Cutting into the arms and ankles is what doctors do to find a vein in that situation when there is so little blood pressure. This is a standard ER procedure. And they didn't feel like they had the time to stop and anesthetized her.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: They did call in helicopters. She was flown to a hospital in the city of Nelson, where she was operated on. For a while, it didn't seem like she was going to survive. She went into a coma, and woke up days later.

segments.speaker: Anonymous
segments.text: And I was in an intensive care unit. And the male nurse was saying, Mom, get in her eye sight. He's coming around. She's coming around. And my mom looked over, and she said, aren't you lucky the doctors saved you?

segments.speaker: Anonymous
segments.text: And I couldn't talk, because I was on life support ventilator for my lungs so that I could breathe. And I indicated for paper and pencil. And I wrote, I saved myself. Underline, underline, underline.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When somebody asks her to tell this story, what happened the day after she was bit by the shark-- or whatever it was-- it's possible for her to get mad all over again. But it usually doesn't come up. She doesn't think about it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And she's fine with her parents. Her relationship with them is pretty much like anybody's. And she understands their actions that day. Everybody moved on.

segments.speaker: Anonymous
segments.text: I mean, they subsequently bought a house just along from where the whole thing happened. And I was very anti that plan.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Wait, they bought a house right near where it happened?

segments.speaker: Anonymous
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Like a vacation house?

segments.speaker: Anonymous
segments.text: Yeah, in this very remote community. And I was like, I'm going to boycott that. But you can't. We went back the next year to the same camping spot.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It was a family with four kids. Nobody was inclined to dwell on the past, including her. Within a year, her dad had started buying joke presents about it-- a necklace with a shark, and a swimmer coming out of its mouth. Or a t-shirt with a cartoon shark bite, fake blood splatters, and a hole-- a real hole in the shirt-- coincidentally, right where her actual bite was.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The fact that she nearly died, that was the past. She wore the shirt and the necklace. And then quietly, after a while, she had enough of it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Coming up, when you're little, you learn that you are supposed to be careful with sharp, dangerous objects. You learn that you are not supposed to put dangerous things into your mouth. In a minute, somebody who ignores both those rules-- really, really ignores them. From Chicago Public Radio and Public Radio International when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life . I'm Ira Glass. Today's program, "What Doesn't Kill You." We have stories of people surviving all kinds of things, and where they end up on the other side of that. We've arrived at Act Three of our show. Act Three, "A Real Nail Biter."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This story is amazing. Because the woman that it's about, I think more than anybody else on today's show, probably should not be around to tell the story. Reporter Jessica Benko tells what happened.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: The woman's name is Cathy. And the thing that almost killed her over and over was a thought. It first appeared one day when she was 12 or 13 years old. She was in a psychiatric institution at the time.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: Cathy asked that I not use her full name on the radio. And she didn't want to discuss certain events of her childhood. She hopes it's enough to describe it as troubled. But she threw violent tantrums as a kid, assaulted her teachers, and even began cutting herself. So Cathy's doctors had convinced her parents an institution might help her. But it was there that the thought first came to her.

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: I was in the quiet room. Quiet rooms are a room that's smaller than the size of a bathroom-- a good-sized bathroom. And it's all concrete. And they have this mattress on the floor that has no springs in it. It's a safety mattress.

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: And I found a nail. At first, I wanted to use it on my arm to cut myself. So I hid it, because I knew if I got caught with it they would take it. And then I got the thought to swallow it.

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: I wanted to feel it go down my throat and go into my stomach.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: Out of anger and frustration, or something else?

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: Nope.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: Curiosity?

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: Out of a compulsion, like the thought. The thought wouldn't leave me alone. And I just did it.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: Cathy says it felt good to swallow the nail. And once it was in her stomach, she felt intense relief. The thought was no longer nagging her. Doctors put her in the hospital and waited for the nail to pass. But once it was gone, the thought returned with increasing frequency, again and again.

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: It was horrible. I was tortured. I literally was tortured in my mind. I've swallowed pencils, hundreds of pencils, multiple toothbrushes, nails, a plastic fork, knives, two antennas-- radio antennas. I swallowed a chess piece, a book bracket. I don't know what it's called, the thing that goes on a shelf, it holds the shelf. Oh, yeah, battery and glass.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: All of this sounds intolerably painful. But for Cathy, it was even more agonizing when she wasn't able to swallow something, when she wasn't able to appease the thought. Cathy told my producer Brian Reed and me about one day when she snatched a straw from the common area of the psych ward. She hid it in her bra, hoping to swallow it the next chance she got. But the staff strip-searched her before she could do it.

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: And they found it on me. And I flipped. I just lost control. I started banging my head on the mirror in the bathroom where they strip-searched me, saying, please don't take it. You're going to kill me. You don't understand how much this-- I got to have it. And they ended up restraining me, and putting me in restraints, and giving me injections until I fell asleep.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: Why were you so upset?

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: Because I thought I was going to die. I thought my mother was going to die.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: Cathy isn't using metaphor here. She genuinely believed this irrational thought that if she didn't swallow the object she had fixated on, she or her mother would die. She says having the object inside her felt like a protection.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: Cathy was given a lot of diagnoses over the years. But doctors believe her swallowing was a symptom of obsessive-compulsive disorder. This is the same disorder that causes people who are afraid of germs to wash their hands incessantly, or others who are worried about a fire to check the stove dozens of times before they can leave the house. Cathy's fear about her or her mother's safety was a more extreme and illogical version of this.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: Doctors didn't have a good cure. No matter what they tried-- therapy, drugs, repeated electroshock treatments-- they could not stop the thought from torturing Cathy. All they could do was try to stop Cathy from hurting herself. She couldn't be trusted on her own, so she was permanently institutionalized and put in four-point restraints.

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: Four-point restraints is when they tie leather down to the bed, and they have handcuffs on the feet, and on the legs, on the arms.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: On top of this, Cathy was constantly supervised by one, and sometimes even two staff members. But that didn't stop her from swallowing things. By law, every eight hours staff had to let her walk around for 15 minutes. Those 15 minutes were Cathy's chance to act.

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: And this is where I would scout things. So I would see what I wanted. And then I wouldn't sleep that night. I'd plan it to a T. It's like playing Stratego, but playing for, like, 24 hours without winning or without losing, but in the end knowing you're going to win.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: She had to win. Because every time she focused in on a new object, the fear that something horrible might happen was reignited.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: Can you tell us about the time you swallowed a knife?

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: Which one?

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: Uh, I don't know.

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: Just pick one?

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: How many times have you swallowed knives?

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: Four.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: Cathy never got her hands on a real metal knife, just the plastic ones they used in the hospital. But the results weren't so different. A quick warning, what Cathy describes in the next minute or so is graphic. You might want to turn down the volume if you're sensitive.

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: I took a knife out of the kitchen. And I put it in my bra. And I asked if I could go to the bathroom. They let me go to the bathroom by myself. I went in, and I went to the bathroom. I swallowed the knife.

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: I started bleeding out of my mouth. Well, my throat was bleeding. And I couldn't breathe right. I was going [GASPING]. I couldn't get a deep breath in.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: Did it hurt right away when it was cutting your esophagus?

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: Yeah. I had a hard time getting it down, because it was cutting me as I was putting it down.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: And you didn't think, oh, my gosh, I might die?

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: No, it's not my thought at all. I kept thinking I had to get it down.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: And you didn't think, OK, I just can't? I need to pull it out.

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: No. I never thought that. Nope.

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: I got a fever of 106. And they saw the hole in my throat. And then they immediately did surgery. And I was in ICU for three weeks. And I couldn't eat because the hole was in my-- it needed repair. And I almost died then.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: This wasn't even the closest Cathy came to dying. Once-- I'm sorry this is a little graphic-- she sneezed while swallowing a radio antenna. And it became lodged dangerously close to her brain stem. Doctors had to put her in a medically induced coma while they figured out how to extract it.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: Over the years, Cathy had more than 500 endoscopies, where surgeons inserted a tube down her throat and pulled the item out through it. She had more than a dozen invasive surgeries to remove objects and repair tears and holes in her stomach, intestines, and esophagus. One of Cathy's doctors told us she almost single-handedly trained an entire generation of surgical residents at his hospital's ER. Things got so bad that after Cathy turned 18, hospital staff went in front of a judge to get permission to put her in a straitjacket.

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: No hospital wanted to keep me longer than they had to. So they shipped me around every six months, because I was a liability.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: Did you have any thoughts at that time about what your future was looking like?

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: I didn't have a future. I didn't see a future. I wanted to die. I didn't have a way to die. I was in a straitjacket. I laid in a bed.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: What did you think about when you were in a straitjacket, laying in bed day after day?

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: If I didn't have something on my mind to swallow, I don't remember thinking anything. I would just exist.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: When Cathy was 21, she was transferred to yet another new facility-- Taunton State Hospital. She was so heavily drugged when she arrived, she didn't wake up for about a week. And when she did, her muscles were so atrophied from being restrained she couldn't hold up her head or lift her arms.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: But Cathy says this hospital, Taunton, was different. The doctors and staff were willing to give her a chance. They set up a system of rewards she could work toward. Each day she went without swallowing something, she was allowed one hour out of the straitjacket.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: They helped her build muscle tone back in her arms by walking her hands up and down the walls. They showed her a bit of kindness. After a winter storm, they brought her a snowball, something she hadn't felt in about 10 years.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: And it was at Taunton that Cathy had a chance encounter that changed her life. Her regular psychiatrist went on vacation, and another doctor filled in for him. He was familiar with a relatively unknown surgery for extreme cases of OCD that he thought might help Cathy. It was a controversial procedure, mostly because when people hear about brain surgery on mentally ill patients, they immediately think of a lobotomy.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: This wasn't a lobotomy. It was much more high-tech and precise than that. But it would mean destroying a small section of Cathy's brain. The idea was that surgeons could burn out a piece of the circuit they believed was malfunctioning-- the circuit that communicated between the emotional and logical parts of Cathy's brain.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: Only one hospital in the country offered the procedure regularly. And it happened to be near Cathy-- Massachusetts General. They had been doing it for decades. And they had found that the risks were low. More than half of the OCD patients who got the surgery improved. And for those that didn't, the side effects were minor.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: So Cathy agreed to try it. It took about two hours. And amazingly, after she got out of the surgery, she immediately felt different. Her urge to swallow had vanished completely.

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: In the beginning I was weary. I'm like, is it really gone? And then I swallowed something, like, two months after I had the procedure. It wasn't that I had the urge. I was so used to swallowing that it was so odd that I didn't feel the urge to swallow. And I'm like, well, maybe I should just swallow something.

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: I'm like, something's missing in my life, you know? It was like an old friend. But after I did it, I'm like, this isn't me. I don't want this.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: That feeling lasted almost a year, until Cathy relapsed. The obsession came back. And she started swallowing again. So doctors did a second surgery and destroyed a little more of her brain. Again, Cathy woke up and the thought was gone. Again, she moved forward warily, not sure if it would last.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: As the months passed, she began earning more freedom in the psych hospital. She was out of the straitjacket for good. Staff let her walk around the grounds of the hospital freely.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: But recovery wasn't easy. Even moments that should have been exciting were challenging instead. Like when she went home for the first time. After spending 10 years confined, mostly in restraints, to mental institutions, she was allowed to go to her mom's house for dinner.

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: It was odd because there were knives. There were all these things that I saw that I'm not used to seeing. Because we had filet mignon and rice pilaf. And it was an odd feeling to cut my steak with a steak knife.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: Did it make you nervous?

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: Yeah. Yeah. I don't know how to explain it. I'm like, a sharp knife. Then I'm like, oh my God.

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: [DOOR CLOSING]

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: This is a little messy, if you don't mind mess.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: More than a decade later, Cathy's showing us around her apartment. When she first moved out on her own, she was 28. Though she essentially had the life skills of a 13-year-old. She had to learn how to cook, how to clean. Her doctor sent someone to teach her how to shower by herself.

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: For like the first month, I probably didn't sleep during the night at all because I had the freedom. I wasn't told to go to bed. So I was just basking in the glory of smoking cigarettes and drinking coffee all night. For like a month I did that. And I would sleep during the day, just because I could.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: Did the world feel foreign to you?

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: It felt big, enormous.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: Since then, Cathy's earned her GED and has taken a few classes at community college. These days, she checks in with her therapist every six months or so. She has a good life. She's funny, easy to talk to.

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: You really don't want to see my bedroom.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: She shares this apartment with her boyfriend of eight years. There's an extra bedroom for her nieces and nephews to stay in when they visit. It's also where Cathy and her boyfriend keep the fishing rods they use on their boat each weekend. There are framed pictures of her family and friends, toys for the kids, and of course, toothbrushes, and forks, and knives.

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: Every single one of these things that are my house I cherish-- every single one of them. I collect pens now.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: Pens?

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: Pens. I have a whole jar of pens over there because they wouldn't allow me to have them for so many years. And now I can have them. And they don't torture me. So I collect them just to say where I've been and where I am now.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: We went over to the desk in the corner of her living room. Cathy picked up a mug filled with pens.

segments.speaker: Cathy
segments.text: They're just different kinds of pens.

segments.speaker: Jessica Benko
segments.text: One came from TD Bank, one from the Institution for Savings. A friend gave her another. Now she can take one out of her collection and jot down a grocery list or a note to her boyfriend.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Jessica Benko in New York.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act Four, "The Sweet Year After." In the aftermath of some terrible incident that nearly kills you, turns out things can be kind of great. Tim Kreider explains how.

segments.speaker: Tim Kreidor
segments.text: 17 years ago, I was stabbed in the throat. This is kind of a long story, and less interesting than it sounds. Except for the 10 or 15 minutes during which it looked like I was about to die, which I would prefer not to relive, getting stabbed wasn't even among the worst experiences of my life. In fact, it was one of the best things that ever happened to me.

segments.speaker: Tim Kreidor
segments.text: After my unsuccessful murder, I wasn't unhappy for an entire year. Winston Churchill's description of the exhilaration of being shot at without result is verifiably true. I'm not claiming to have been continuously euphoric the whole time. It's just that during that grace period, nothing much could bother me or get me down.

segments.speaker: Tim Kreidor
segments.text: The horrible thing I'd always dreaded was going to happen to me had finally happened. I figured I was off the hook for a while. In a parallel universe only two millimeters away, the distance between my carotid and the stiletto, I would have been flown home in the cargo hold instead of in coach.

segments.speaker: Tim Kreidor
segments.text: I started brewing my own dandelion wine in a big Amish crock. I listened to old one hit wonders, much too embarrassing to name in public. And I developed a strange new laugh that's stayed with me to this day-- a loud, raucous barking thing. It makes people in bars or restaurants look over for a second to make sure I'm not about to open up on the crowd with a weapon.

segments.speaker: Tim Kreidor
segments.text: Not for one passing moment did it occur to me that God must have spared my life for some purpose. Even if I had been the type who was prone to such notions, I would have been disabused of it by the heavy-handed coincidence of the Oklahoma City bombing occurring on the same day I spent in a recuperative coma. If there is some divine plan that requires my survival and the deaths of all those children in daycare, I respectfully decline to participate.

segments.speaker: Tim Kreidor
segments.text: What I had been was not blessed or chosen, but lucky. Which is not to turn my nose up at luck. It's better to be lucky than just about anything else in life. And if you're hearing this now, you're among the lucky, too.

segments.speaker: Tim Kreidor
segments.text: You'd like to think that nearly getting killed would be a permanently life-altering experience. But getting stabbed was like a lightning strike-- over almost as soon as it happened, and the illumination didn't last. You can't feel crazily grateful to be alive your whole life anymore than you can stay passionately in love forever, or grieve forever for that matter. Time makes us all betray ourselves and get back to the busy work of living.

segments.speaker: Tim Kreidor
segments.text: It's easy now to dismiss that year as nothing more than the same sort of shaky, hysterical high you'd feel after being clipped by a taxi. But you could also try to think of it as a rare glimpse of reality, being jolted out of a lifelong stupor. I can't recapture that feeling of euphoric gratitude any more than I can really remember the mortal terror I felt when I was pretty sure I had about four minutes to live. But I know that it really happened, that that state of grace is accessible to us, even if I only blundered across it once and never find my way back.

segments.speaker: Tim Kreidor
segments.text: At my cabin on the Chesapeake Bay, I'll sometimes see bald eagles swoop up from the water with wriggling little fish in their talons. And whenever they accidentally drop their catch, I like to imagine that fish trying to tell his friends about his own near-death experience, a perspective so unprecedented there are no words in the fish language to describe it. For a short time, he was outside the world. He could see forever. There's so much more than they knew. But he's glad to be back.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Tim Kreidor reading an excerpt from his book of essays and cartoons with the really wonderful name We Learn Nothing.

segments.speaker: Anonymous
segments.text: I'm on fire. I'm burning up.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Well, understandable, I guess. I'm Ira Glass. Back next week with more stories of This American Life.
